opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one of the problems we have in machine learning is that we've been fairly sloppy about how we talk about uncertainty. For years the field has leaned on this two-way split between aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Aleatoric is the irreducible noise in the world, and epistemic is the uncertainty that comes from our lack of knowledge, which in principle more data could reduce. That's a useful starting point, but it hides a lot of important distinctions.

What I like about the paper by Cornelia Gruber and her colleagues is that they come at it from a statistician's perspective. They ask very carefully: what is the actual generative story? Where in the pipeline from the world, to the data, to the model, to the prediction does uncertainty enter? Once you lay it out that way, you see there are many more sources than the two-bucket picture suggests.

For example, there's uncertainty about whether your model class is even correct, which is model specification uncertainty. There's uncertainty in estimating the parameters given finite data. There's uncertainty from how the data were collected: sampling, measurement error, label noise. And there's the question of whether the deployment data will look like the training data at all. Statisticians have thought about these things for a long time, and machine learning people often reinvent them, or worse, lump them all together.

The practical payoff is that different sources call for different remedies. If your uncertainty comes from too little data in some region of the input space, collecting more data there helps. If it comes from measurement noise, more data of the same kind won't fix it, and you may need a better sensor or a better labeling process. If it comes from model misspecification, you need to change the model. And if it's distribution shift, you need monitoring and some way to detect novelty. If you can't tell these apart, you can't make good decisions about what to do next.

So I recommend the paper because it gives a clean, principled vocabulary for these distinctions. It's very readable, and I think it can help the machine learning community be more precise. That precision matters a lot when we're trying to build systems that know when they don't know, which is central to safe and reliable deployment in high-stakes settings.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the main reason is that the machine learning community has, in some sense, reinvented a lot of ideas about uncertainty that statisticians have been thinking about for a very long time, and we've done it with our own vocabulary and our own somewhat muddled set of distinctions. The paper that Gruber and her colleagues wrote is really an attempt to step back and say, okay, where does uncertainty actually come from when you're building a predictive model?

The thing I find most valuable is that they don't just stop at the aleatoric versus epistemic split that everybody in machine learning talks about. That split is useful, but it's pretty coarse. They break epistemic uncertainty down further. There's uncertainty because you have a finite sample, so your parameter estimates are noisy. There's uncertainty because your model class may not contain the true function, what statisticians call model misspecification. And then there's uncertainty that comes from the whole process upstream of the learning algorithm: how the data were collected, whether there's selection bias, whether the labels themselves are noisy or defined in a way that doesn't quite match what you care about. Those are very different problems, and they call for very different remedies. If your problem is a small sample, collecting more data helps. If your problem is misspecification, more data just makes you more confidently wrong.

The other thing I like is that it's honest about the fact that this decomposition isn't always clean. Whether something counts as aleatoric or epistemic depends on what features you have access to and what you're willing to model. If you add a new feature, some of what looked like irreducible noise suddenly becomes predictable. So the boundary moves, and the paper is clear-eyed about that rather than pretending these are fixed categories of nature.

And frankly, it's written in a way that a machine learning person can read without having to translate everything. A lot of the statistics literature on this is scattered across decades of work on calibration, on prediction intervals, on model selection. Having it pulled together in one place, with the statistical view explained in terms we recognize, is just a very good service to the field. I think if more people read it before they started slapping a Bayesian neural network or an ensemble on their problem and calling that "uncertainty quantification," we'd have a lot fewer confused papers.

astra-6.text:
I recommend it because it gives us a broader way to think about uncertainty than the distinction we often make between aleatoric uncertainty—the randomness in the observations—and epistemic uncertainty, which comes from what we don’t know about the model.

Those are useful categories, but they’re not the whole story. We have a sequence of choices: how we collect the data, how we represent the problem, what model family we choose, and how we estimate its parameters. Each of those can introduce uncertainty. A statistical perspective helps us ask which of those sources our uncertainty estimates actually capture.

That’s the key point for me: an uncertainty estimate is conditional on assumptions. You can have a model that appears very confident, but that confidence doesn’t necessarily account for whether you chose an appropriate model or whether the data you’ll encounter in deployment resemble your training data. The paper provides a useful framework for thinking more carefully about what we know, what we don’t know, and what our methods are leaving out.

sol-6.1.text:
I recommend it because it gives you a broader view of uncertainty than the distinction we often make in machine learning between aleatoric uncertainty—randomness in the observations—and epistemic uncertainty, which comes from what we don’t know. That distinction is useful, but it doesn’t tell the whole story.

There’s uncertainty in the data you collect, in the assumptions you make, in the model you choose, and in the parameters you estimate. And then there’s the question of whether the conditions where you deploy the model match the conditions where you trained it. You can quantify one of those sources very carefully and still miss something important.

The statistician’s perspective encourages you to ask, “What is this uncertainty estimate actually accounting for, and what is it leaving out?” I think that’s a very useful habit, especially when we want to use machine learning systems to make consequential decisions.
